Chapter 01 · Introductions & landing sites

Meet Spirit and Opportunity

Two robotic explorers. Two distant landing sites. One enormous question: did ancient Mars have liquid water?

Spirit
Hi! I am Spirit.
Opportunity
And I am Opportunity.
Both
We are twins! We were born on Earth, but in 2004, we went to the Red Planet, Mars, and we're still there. We went there to find answers to the question: Was there water on Mars?
Spirit
But before knowing what we discovered, we'll introduce you to ourselves in more detail! What do rovers consist of?

Our bodies

A body is a strong structure that protects our vital organs, which are computers and electronics.

Our brains

Computers that process information.

Keeping warm

Temperature controls, such as internal heaters. Mars is usually so cold.

Our eyes

A neck and head, where our eyes and other senses are placed. Our eyes are cameras. We can see what we see!

Our arm

An arm much like a human arm.

Six wheels

Wheels to move freely. Every one of us has six wheels.

Our energy

We have things in common with the human body structure, but unfortunately, we don't sleep to obtain energy. We have batteries and solar panels.

Our antennas

We use antennas for speaking and listening, and to be able to communicate with engineers on Earth.
Mission fact: Spirit landed on January 3, 2004, at Gusev Crater. Opportunity landed on January 24, 2004, at Meridiani Planum.
Opportunity
Let's return to our journey on Mars.
Spirit
We went to two different locations on Mars. Our separation was not easy for us, but we adapted to it.
Opportunity
I landed at Meridiani Planum.
Spirit
And I landed at Gusev Crater.

Spirit · Gusev Crater

Landing date: January 3, 2004
Exploration included the Columbia Hills and the Comanche outcrop.

Opportunity · Meridiani Planum

Landing date: January 24, 2004
Exploration included Eagle Crater, Fram Crater and much farther beyond.
Think about it: Why send two similar rovers to different places? Because exploring different rocks and landscapes can reveal different chapters of a planet's history.
Chapter 02 · Discoveries of ancient water

Two different watery worlds

The rovers found clues that ancient Mars had more than one kind of watery environment.

Opportunity
I found something interesting on Mars, specifically near Fram Crater. I found blueberries!
Opportunity
Not the kind you eat!
Opportunity
They are small, spherical deposits of the mineral hematite, which form in water. They are called blueberries. This proves that water soaked this area on Mars in the ancient past. But it was not the water we drink; it was acidic water that made life even harder on its surface.
Spirit
Oh, I also found something interesting in a place called Comanche. I found rocks there that are 10 times richer in magnesium and iron carbonates than any other Martian rocks studied before.
Spirit
This means that this place on Mars was warm and wet. This warm and wet environment could have supported life much better than the acidic environment you found.

Opportunity's clue

Hematite-rich concretions and evidence of ancient acidic groundwater at Meridiani Planum.

Spirit's clue

Carbonate-rich rocks at Comanche, pointing to ancient wet, near-neutral conditions.

Explorer's question

Which rover discovered the famous hematite-rich “blueberries” near Fram Crater?

Another explorer's question

What did the carbonate-rich rocks at Comanche suggest?

Remember: Neither discovery proves that life existed on Mars. They help scientists understand whether ancient environments could have supported microbial life.
Chapter 03 · Gypsum, clay, silica & craters

More secrets beneath the surface

Opportunity
I found evidence that Mars was once more hospitable to life than it is today! I found bright-toned veins of gypsum in the rocks near the rim of Endeavour Crater.
Spirit
What is a gypsum vein?
Opportunity
A gypsum vein is a thin crack or fracture inside a rock that is filled with the light-colored mineral gypsum. It forms when mineral-rich underground water containing calcium and sulfate flows through underground rock fractures, leaving behind solid mineral deposits over time.
Spirit
So, that is evidence of water?
Opportunity
Exactly! This mineral vein is called Homestake.
Opportunity
I also explored Pillinger Point, on the western rim of Endeavour Crater. The clay minerals found there formed in neutral-pH water—water that was much less acidic than the water in some other ancient Martian environments. This area once had some of the friendliest conditions for ancient microbial life.
Spirit
That's wonderful! One day, while I was wandering near Home Plate, my wheel churned up the soil, and I found more than 90% pure silica!
Spirit
On Earth, this kind of silica is often found in hot springs or hot steam vents. Isn't that funny? Such places can be happy homes for ancient microbes—and perhaps they were on Mars, too.
Opportunity
I love ancient microbes, but do you know what I love more? Craters!
Opportunity
I visited and studied the geology of well over 100 impact craters of all sizes. I learned about the lives of craters and studied how they form and erode through time.
Spirit
Craters?! Aren't these related to volcanoes?
Spirit
One day, I found evidence of an ancient explosion at Home Plate. Heated underground water may have produced powerful steam eruptions and contributed to explosive volcanic activity. Despite their violence, these extreme conditions can support microbial life on Earth, so maybe they did on Mars, too.
Opportunity
Your discovery is wonderful! But when I said craters, I didn't mean the craters related to volcanoes. The craters I discovered were impact craters. The main difference between them is that impact craters are made by space rocks crashing down from above, while volcanic craters are formed by volcanic activity from below.
Spirit
Oh! Now I understand the difference.

Impact craters

Form when asteroids, meteoroids or other space objects strike a surface.

Volcanic craters

Form through volcanic processes, such as eruptions and the collapse of material around a volcanic vent.
Scientific note: Spirit found silica-rich soil near Home Plate. NASA describes the Home Plate deposits as evidence of an ancient explosion; scientists have considered volcanic and impact-related explanations. The silica may have formed through hot-spring or steam-vent processes.
Final chapter · Their journeys & legacy

The story isn't forgotten.

Opportunity
Do you know that I really respect Spirit? In my opinion, Spirit is much better than me because his discoveries are useful.
Spirit
Don't say that! You are better than me. I worked for 6 years, while you worked for more than 14 years. I captured only 124,838 raw images, while you captured 217,594 raw images. I travelled 4.8 miles, while you travelled 28.06 miles and held the off-Earth rover driving-distance record until October 11, 2026. I climbed a steepest slope of 30 degrees, while you climbed a steepest slope of 32 degrees. You are the best!
Opportunity
The judgment is for our friends, the readers! Which one of us do you think is better: me, my twin, or both of us?
Opportunity
This conversation was life-giving as we remembered our discoveries before my twin's mission ended in 2010 and before I lost communication with Earth in 2018, when a planet-wide dust storm blanketed my location on Mars and blocked sunlight from reaching my solar panels.
Spirit
Yeah, you're right. Our friends, if any of you become astronauts and come to Mars, don't forget to visit us!

Your turn, explorer

Which rover do you think was better?

Mission endings: Spirit's final communication came in March 2010, and NASA ended recovery efforts in 2011. Opportunity's final communication was received on June 10, 2018; NASA declared the mission over in February 2019.
A new record: Opportunity drove 28.06 miles (45.16 km). On October 11, 2026, NASA's Perseverance rover passed that distance, reaching 28.10 miles (45.22 km).
